catalog_quote: Ewe is a tone language. Phonetically, all the dialects have high, mid, and low tones, which also combine to yield six contour tones. Phonologically, it has a high and nonhigh tone, both of which are dependent on the environment. Thus nonhigh tone is realized as mid in a root noun that has a voiceless obstruent or sonorant, and low before a voiced obstruent. High tone is realized as high before a voiceless obstruent and mid before a voiced obstruent. Anlo also has a phonologically conditioned extrahigh tone, while Adangbe has an extralow tone that occurs on the utterance-final interrogative particle.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Adangbe, treated as a dialect of Ewe, is a tone language (underlying high vs non-high, consonant-conditioned surface high/mid/low, plus an Adangbe-specific extra-low tone on the utterance-final interrogative particle); the source makes no statement about word stress. Maddieson & Gandour 1974 (entries 9459-9460, second-hand from Sprigge 1972 and Sprigge & Ford 1972) likewise report only a two-toneme system for Adangbe Ewe.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; the only Adangbe-specific remark is the extra-low tone on the utterance-final interrogative particle.
new_statements.domain_note: Encyclopedia article on the Ewe dialect cluster as a whole; the Adangbe remark is second-hand (ultimately from Sprigge 1967). No word- or phrase-level stress claim is made. The first-hand description of this lect (Sprigge 1967, 156 pp. on tone) could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog adan1248 (Eweic, Western Gbe) is the Ewe variety spoken by the Agotime/Adangbe people around Kpetoe on the Ghana-Togo border east of Ho; its sole Glottolog description, Sprigge 1967, calls it 'the Adangbe dialect of Ewe' (Sprigge & Ford 1972: 'spoken in Togo'), and Capo 2000 lists 'Adangbe' (elsewhere 'Adan') among the ~60 Gbe lects. Not to be confused with (a) Dangme/Adangme adan1247 (Ga-Dangme), nor (b) the Agotime's heritage Ga-Dangme lect described by Rapp 1943 'Die Adangme-Ga-Mundart von Agotime in Togo' (Afrika 2:4-58), which older Ethnologue-derived sources and the English Wikipedia stub (which files 'Agotime' under Ka-Togo/Kposo-Ahlo) conflate with this code. All accessible linguistic mentions (Clements 1974, Essegbey 2009, Ameka 2001, Hyman ed. 1973) treat Adangbe as a dialect of Ewe and draw their data from Sprigge 1967.
